Rotate a runner token

Swarm secrets are immutable. To rotate a token, create a second secret and swap it into the service that holds it. On Linux, that is the token-proxy service for a single-task class: one replica, so the swap takes seconds, and the runners are not touched. For a persistent class and on Windows it is the service of the class itself. The rolling update replaces one replica at a time, and busy runners finish their job first. The update is serial per replica: the shipped stack files set update_config.parallelism: 1, and a busy replica is replaced only after its job ends, which takes up to the grace period of 5 hours and 5 minutes. A service with N replicas can therefore take up to N times that long to finish the swap. To shorten it, raise update_config.parallelism in the stack file, or pass --update-parallelism <number> to docker service update for one update (0 replaces every replica at once).

  1. Create a new token in CircleCI. Keep the old token until the swap is complete.

    $ circleci runner token create <namespace>/linux-default --nickname "linux-default-<date>"

  2. Create a secret with the new token. Use a new name, such as linux-default-token-v2.

    printf 'New token (hidden): '; stty -echo; IFS= read -r TOKEN; stty echo; echo
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] && printf 'api:\n auth_token: %s\n' "$TOKEN" | docker secret create linux-default-token-v2 -
unset TOKEN

  3. Swap the secrets in the service. On Linux, for a single-task class, swap it in the proxy. Keep the target: the proxy names a class after the file <service>-token, and a new name makes a new class that no runner belongs to:

    $ docker service update \
 --secret-rm linux-default-token \
 --secret-add source=linux-default-token-v2,target=linux-default-token,uid=65534,gid=65534,mode=0400 \
 runners_token-proxy

    The proxy restarts and reads the state from proxy-state, so runners that have not claimed may claim again. Recycle runners only when the start log says no state or state lost: docker service update --force --update-parallelism 0 runners_<service> for each affected Linux class, or wait for their idle timeout. On Windows, remove only the refused containers (Replace refused runners on Windows), or wait. Refer to Restart the proxy.

    On Linux, for a persistent class, swap it in the service itself:

    $ docker service update \
 --secret-rm linux-persistent-token \
 --secret-add source=linux-persistent-token-v2,target=circleci_runner_config.yaml,uid=2000,gid=2000,mode=0400 \
 runners_linux-persistent

    On Windows, a single-task class is swapped in the proxy as well (secrets have no uid, gid, or mode, and the target is the file of the class in the proxy):

    docker service update `
 --secret-rm windows-default-token `
 --secret-add source=windows-default-token-v2,target=windows-default-token `
 runners_token-proxy-windows

    On Windows, for the persistent class, swap it in the service itself, with the target circleci_runner_config.yaml.

  4. Wait until the update completes. The state is completed:

    $ docker service inspect --format '{{.UpdateStatus.State}}' runners_token-proxy

  5. Record the new name in your stack file: change source: and the entry under the top-level secrets: (for the proxy, the source: of the class under token-proxy). A later docker stack deploy from the old file then does not revert the swap.

  6. Revoke the old token in CircleCI, and remove the old secret.

    $ circleci runner token list --resource-class <namespace>/linux-default
$ circleci runner token delete <token ID>
$ docker secret rm linux-default-token

If a token leaked

Do not swap first. Until the old token is deleted in CircleCI, it stays valid for anyone who holds it. For a class that holds its token in its runners (a persistent class, or Windows), the swap above can take up to N times 5 hours and 5 minutes for N replicas, because it replaces one replica at a time and each busy replica finishes its job first. For a single-task class on Linux the swap is in the proxy and takes seconds, but the leak itself means that someone reached the proxy’s node or the secret, so read the end of this section. Delete the token as soon as its replacement exists:

  1. Create the new token, and the secret with the new token. Use the steps 1 and 2 above. Nothing uses the new secret yet.

  2. Delete the old token at once.

    $ circleci runner token list --resource-class <namespace>/linux-default
$ circleci runner token delete <token ID>

    CircleCI stops accepting the old token for new claims, so nobody can start a runner on the class with it. Jobs that already run continue until they end. A proxy that still holds the old secret, or idle runners of a persistent class or Windows that still hold it, fail with 401 until the swap, so the class claims no new jobs until step 3 completes.

  3. Swap the secrets. For a single-task class on Linux, swap it in the proxy with the command of step 3 above, and replace the idle runners (docker service update --force --update-parallelism 0 runners_<service>; on Windows, as in Replace refused runners on Windows). For the other classes, replace every replica at once so that the class recovers soon:

    $ docker service update --update-parallelism 0 \
 --secret-rm linux-default-token \
 --secret-add source=linux-default-token-v2,target=circleci_runner_config.yaml,uid=2000,gid=2000,mode=0400 \
 runners_linux-default

    Each replica still finishes the job that it runs before Swarm replaces it. On Windows, drop uid, gid, and mode, and expect the update to end a running job after about 5 seconds: rerun those jobs. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container.

  4. Do steps 4 and 5 above (wait for the update, record the new name in your stack file), and remove the old secret with docker secret rm linux-default-token. Then look for what the leaked token did: the runner inventory in CircleCI for names you do not know, and the jobs that ran on the class.

A leaked token of a single-task class on Linux did not come from a job in a runner container, because those hold no token. Look at who can read Swarm secrets (the docker group on a manager), at the node that runs the proxy, and at the backups of the managers. Rotate the tokens of every class whose secret that path reached, because the proxy holds all of them.

Drain a node for patching

A node drain (docker node update --availability drain) stops the tasks of a node and keeps new tasks away. On Linux, Swarm sends SIGTERM and waits for the grace period, so a running job finishes. On Windows, a drain kills a running job after about 5 seconds, so use the procedure for a Windows node below. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container. Restarting the Docker daemon stops every running container, because live restore does not work in Swarm mode, so always empty the node before you patch Docker or reboot.

$ docker node update --availability drain <node name>
$ docker node ps <node name>

Wait until docker node ps shows no running tasks. Swarm starts the replacement tasks on other nodes at once. If the other nodes lack capacity, the replacements stay Pending until the drained tasks exit. Patch and reboot the node, and then return it to service:

$ docker node update --availability active <node name>

Tasks do not move back to the node by themselves. Single-task replicas restart after every job, so new tasks spread over the nodes again within a short time. Patch managers one at a time, so the cluster keeps its quorum. Refer to Managers and quorum.

A Windows node

A drain kills a busy Windows container, and no setting changes that. Use pause, which keeps new tasks away and stops nothing:

$ docker node update --availability pause <node name>
$ docker node ps <node name> --filter desired-state=running

A running job keeps its container. Each replica that finishes its job exits, and Swarm starts its replacement on another node, so the node empties by itself. An idle replica exits only at its idle timeout (1 hour in the shipped files), and it can still claim a job until then. So the upper bound is the idle timeout plus the longest job. Wait until the second command prints nothing, then drain the node (no job is left to kill), patch it, and set it active.

No unattended changes

An update that restarts the Docker daemon or the node by itself ends every container on it, and on Windows that kills the jobs. Switch off everything that patches or restarts a node without you, on every node:

  • Windows. Set the Windows Update policy to download and notify, so that it never installs an update or restarts the node on its own. Install and reboot only in the procedure above.
  • Debian and Ubuntu. Set Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot "false". Hold the Docker packages, because an upgrade of docker-ce restarts the daemon: sudo apt-mark hold docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io, and sudo apt-mark unhold ... for the planned upgrade. Set needrestart to list only ($nrconf{restart} = 'l';), so that it does not restart the daemon after another upgrade.
  • RHEL and its clones. Turn off the automatic installation of dnf-automatic (or limit it to a download), and hold the Docker packages with a version lock of your package manager.

Do the planned upgrade with the node emptied, as above.

The node of the proxy

Draining the node that runs token-proxy stops the proxy, and the placement decides what follows. A proxy that is pinned to a labelled node stays Pending until that node is active again, and then starts there with its state. No claim is possible in between, so choose a quiet period, and patch that node last. A proxy with the default placement moves to another manager, and its state stays behind (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves). Draining every manager, or the only node that can run the proxy, stops every claim: keep one node undrained for it (the warning in Multi-Node Clusters).

Stop a busy Windows container

On Linux, a stop lets the running job finish. On Windows, stopping a busy container from outside kills its job after about 5 seconds.

The normal flow is not affected. A job finishes, the runner exits, and the container ends cleanly. Swarm then starts a new container for the next job. Nothing stops a container from outside, so no job is lost.

Only a stop of a busy container from outside kills the job. When Docker stops a container, Windows sends the shutdown event to it. The runner turns the event into SIGTERM and drains (a runner drain): it accepts no new job and lets the running job finish. On Server Core, Windows waits only the time in the registry value WaitToKillServiceTimeout before it ends the processes. The default is 5 seconds, whatever docker stop -t or stop_grace_period says. The container then exits with the code 3221225786 (0xC000013A), and the job dies with it. Every one of these actions stops containers in this way:

  • A rolling update, with docker stack deploy or docker service update: a deploy or an update.
  • docker service scale to a lower number: a scale-down.
  • docker node update --availability drain: a node drain.
  • docker stack rm, and a restart of the Docker service.

So roll out changes while the class is idle, or rerun the jobs that were interrupted.

Microsoft describes the same limit in hcsshim pull request 1416 and in Windows-Containers issue 164. Microsoft fixed it only in the containerd shim, and Swarm uses the runtime of the Docker engine, which does not have that fix. The CI of this repository measures the rule in every run: Test-StopHandling.ps1 stops a stock container that runs a fake job of 40 seconds and reports what happens to the job.

Roll out a change when the class is idle

The runner API shows what a class is doing. Use a personal API token, not a resource class token.

$h = @{ 'Circle-Token' = $env:CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN }
$api = 'https://runner.circleci.com' # the runner API of your installation, for CircleCI server
Invoke-RestMethod -Headers $h -Uri "$api/api/v3/runner/tasks/running?resource-class=<namespace>/windows-default"
Invoke-RestMethod -Headers $h -Uri "$api/api/v3/runner/tasks?resource-class=<namespace>/windows-default"

The first call returns running_runner_tasks, and the second returns unclaimed_task_count. Wait for running_runner_tasks to be 0 in a quiet period, and then run docker service update or docker stack deploy. A rolling update replaces one replica at a time and interrupts only that replica. Single-task runners also recycle after every job and at the idle timeout, so an idle class is easy to find. A drain of a node and docker service scale to a lower number kill running jobs in the same way, so wait for an idle class there too. Refer to the runner API reference.

Optional: an image that lets a job finish after a stop (DIY)

You can lift the limit with your own image. The image sets the registry value WaitToKillServiceTimeout once, at build time. The value is in milliseconds, so set at least the longest job that you allow plus a margin. This example uses 18,300,000, which is 5 hours and 5 minutes, the max_run_time of the runner plus 5 minutes:

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022
RUN reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control /v WaitToKillServiceTimeout /t REG_SZ /d 18300000 /f

Note

Set the value at build time. We tested setting it at run time with reg add inside a running container, for example from the first step of a job, and it does not work. Windows reads the value only when the container boots, so a value that you change later has no effect on that container.

Use the image as the image: of the service. The service still mounts the runner and Git and sets PATH, as in the shipped stack file. Build one image for each Server Core tag, push it to a registry that every Windows node can reach, and rebuild it after each Patch Tuesday update of the base image.

Warning

Never use New-Item -Force on an existing registry key, in an image build or in a running container. It replaces the key and deletes its values and subkeys. On the cexecsvc service key, it makes the container fail to start with hcs::System::Start: context deadline exceeded. Use reg add or Set-ItemProperty, which set one value.

An image like this is not part of the default path, and this repository does not build or test it. Before you rely on a long runner drain, test it. Run a job of a few minutes on a node that is not in production, force an update of its service with docker service update --force, and check that the job finishes.

Recycle a class

A forced update replaces every replica of a service, one at a time, each with a runner drain. Use it to move a persistent class to a new runner version, or to reset it.

$ docker service update --force runners_linux-persistent

On Windows, a forced update kills a running job after about 5 seconds, so recycle a Windows class only while it is idle (Stop a busy Windows container).

A persistent class keeps state between jobs, and recycling removes only the container filesystem. The named volume survives, so /home/circleci on Linux and C:\cache on Windows keep their files. To reset the volume as well, scale the service to 0. Then run docker volume rm runners_persistent-home (Linux) or docker volume rm runners_windows-persistent-cache (Windows) on the node that holds the volume, and scale the service back up.

On Linux, the runner of a persistent class does not clean its working directory. The runner user cannot remove files that the job user owns, so the stack sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR to "false". Files from one job stay for the next job until the container is replaced. Start every job on that class with a step that removes what an earlier job left, and recycle the class on a schedule. Refer to Working directory cleanup.

Free disk space

A full disk is the most common way a node stops running jobs, and a full manager disk can break Swarm itself. This section says where the space goes, how to keep it from filling, and what to do when it is full.

Where the space goes

  • Stopped containers. A job runs in the writable layer of its container, and the layer stays until Swarm prunes the task. A slot keeps its running task and up to task-history-limit finished ones, so a class of R replicas can hold R times (1 plus the limit) layers. The default limit of Swarm is 5. A job that leaves gigabytes behind makes this the largest item.
  • Images. Each tag that a job image has had, and each version of your own images, stays on the node until something removes it. docker image prune removes only images with no tag.
  • Logs. The stack files cap the log of each container: 3 files of 20 MB (60 MB) for a runner on both systems and for the Linux proxy, and 10 MB for the Windows proxy. A log goes with its container.
  • The engine of a docker-build node. Images, volumes and build cache that jobs leave there.
  • The Raft log and the state of Swarm, in /var/lib/docker/swarm of each manager, on the same disk as everything else.

Prevent it

  1. Set the task history limit on the cluster. docker swarm update --task-history-limit 2 keeps at most 2 finished tasks for each slot. The single-node setup of linux/setup.sh sets it, and a swarm that you create yourself does not: refer to Create the swarm.

  2. Give Docker its own filesystem, and keep managers free of jobs. Put /var/lib/docker on a separate volume, so that nothing else fills it, and size it for the worst case in the list above: replicas, times the largest workspace, times (1 plus the history limit), plus the images. A manager that carries the proxy label runs no jobs (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves).

  3. Prune the images on every node, on a schedule. Swarm has no command that runs on every node, and a global service with the Docker socket would be root on every node, so use the scheduler of the node (a configuration management tool, or a systemd timer on each Linux node). The first file removes the images that no container uses and that are older than a week, and the second runs it every Sunday:

    # /etc/systemd/system/docker-image-prune.service
[Unit]
Description=Remove unused Docker images older than a week

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/docker image prune --all --force --filter until=168h
    # /etc/systemd/system/docker-image-prune.timer
[Unit]
Description=Weekly removal of unused Docker images

[Timer]
OnCalendar=Sun 03:00
RandomizedDelaySec=1h
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
    $ sudo systemctl daemon-reload
$ sudo systemctl enable --now docker-image-prune.timer

    until filters by the creation time of the image, and not by its last use, and --all skips every image that a container, a stopped one included, still uses. An image that is removed and needed again is pulled again, so a mirror (What needs the internet) must be up. On a node of a docker-build class, add docker builder prune --force --filter until=168h. On Windows, run the same docker image prune command from a scheduled task. The Server Core image and the distributor image are in use while the stack runs, so a prune does not remove them.

  4. Alert on the disk of every node (df -h /var/lib/docker): above 80 percent on a worker, and above 70 percent on a manager (Monitor the cluster).

Warning

Do not run docker volume prune or docker system prune --volumes on a node of this stack. The named volumes hold runner-bin, proxy-state and the persistent classes. A volume that no container uses at that moment, for example a persistent class that you scaled to 0, is deleted with its data. Leave docker container prune to the task history as well, except in an emergency.

When the disk is full

A node with a full disk fails tasks, with no space left on device in the log of the runner or in docker stack ps --no-trunc, and Docker commands on it fail. A full manager disk comes first, because Swarm cannot write its log.

  1. Find out which node: df -h /var/lib/docker on each, and the ERROR column of docker stack ps runners --no-trunc.

  2. Stop it from claiming more jobs. On Linux, drain the node. On Windows, pause it, because a drain kills the running jobs (A Windows node):

    $ docker node update --availability drain <node name>

  3. See what takes the space:

    $ docker system df
$ docker ps -a --size --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.Names}}' | sort -hr | head

  4. Free it, starting with what is cheapest to get back:

    $ docker image prune --all --force
$ docker builder prune --force
$ docker container prune --force

    docker container prune removes the stopped containers of finished tasks, which Swarm does not need. It removes no running container. Do not prune volumes.

  5. If the disk is a manager, check the cluster before you go on: docker node ls and docker service ls must answer, and the proxy must be running (docker service ps runners_token-proxy).

  6. Return the node to service (docker node update --availability active <node name>), set the task history limit if it is not set, and add the scheduled prune above.

Uninstall

  1. Remove the stack. Swarm sends SIGTERM to the tasks, so running jobs get the grace period to finish.

    $ docker stack rm runners

  2. Remove the secrets, and the volumes of persistent classes.

    $ docker secret rm linux-default-token runner-placeholder-token # and the <service>-token of every other class you deployed
$ docker volume rm runners_persistent-home runners_proxy-state

    The volume of the Windows persistent class is runners_windows-persistent-cache, and the Windows proxy keeps its state in runners_proxy-state too.

    The volume runners_runner-bin holds the runner (and Git on Windows) and stays on every node after docker stack rm. Remove it on every node, on Windows after the last container of the stack is gone:

    $ docker volume rm runners_runner-bin

  3. Remove the nodes from the Swarm. Run docker swarm leave on each worker, then docker swarm leave --force on the last manager. No node has files outside Docker to remove.

item.title: Troubleshooting
item.description:
This page lists symptoms with their cause and fix. Start with the state of the tasks and the runner output:

$ docker stack ps runners --no-trunc
$ docker service logs --tail 100 runners_<service>

For the shared CircleCI guidance, refer to Troubleshoot self-hosted runner.

General

A task stays pending

The ERROR column of docker service ps --no-trunc runners_<service> shows no suitable node, and the task stays in the Pending state.

Cause. No node satisfies the task.

  • scheduling constraints not satisfied on N nodes: no node matches the constraints. A label is missing, the OS or architecture differs, or the service needs a worker and the label sits on a manager.
  • insufficient resources on N nodes: the reservations of the replicas exceed what the matching nodes have free. Reservations equal the limits, so extra replicas wait on purpose.
  • An error that mentions max replicas per node: the SSH add-on runs one replica on each node, because a node has one host-mode port 54782. Add nodes, or lower replicas.

Fix. Compare the constraints of the service with the labels of the nodes.

$ docker service inspect --format '{{ json .Spec.TaskTemplate.Placement }}' runners_<service>
$ docker node inspect --format '{{ .Description.Hostname }} {{ .Spec.Labels }}' $(docker node ls -q)

Add the missing label with docker node update --label-add, lower replicas, or lower the reservations. Refer to Labels and constraints.

The container restarts every 10 seconds

docker service ps lists many tasks of one slot, each with task: non-zero exit (80) or (1), started about 10 seconds apart.

Cause. The runner or the entrypoint exits at start-up because of a configuration error. Swarm restarts the container after the restart delay. It never gives up and never backs off, so the loop runs until you fix the cause. The log line names the problem:

Log text Cause
api.auth_token must be set The secret has an empty token, or the wrong structure
runner.name must be set CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME is missing
runner.name must contain only letters, numbers, .()_-, and spaces The name has other characters, or exceeds 64 characters because of a long hostname or class name
--runner.mode must be one of "continuous","single-task" CIRCLECI_RUNNER_MODE has another value
error parsing config file, or a missing file (exit code 1) The secret is not valid YAML, or it is not attached with the target circleci_runner_config.yaml
circleci-runner-entrypoint: error: ... The entrypoint found a missing prerequisite, or no runner. Refer to the Linux entries below

Fix. Correct the stack file or the secret, and deploy again. To stop the loop meanwhile, run docker service scale runners_<service>=0.

The restart delay is a pause between starts, not a back-off. Swarm creates the replacement task at once and starts its container after the delay, so the containers start 10 to 12 seconds apart. A max_attempts value in restart_policy would end the loop, but then the runner never recovers by itself after you fix the cause, so the stack does not set it. Alert on exit code 80 instead.

Error: secret not found

docker stack deploy fails with secret not found: linux-default-token.

Cause. A service references an external secret that does not exist. Every service in the file needs its <service>-token secret, and on Linux every runner service also needs runner-placeholder-token.

Fix. Create the secret, or delete the service from your copy of the stack file together with its entries under secrets: and networks:. On Windows, runners.yaml needs only windows-default-token, and each add-on stack file (custom-image.yaml, persistent.yaml, docker-build.yaml, ssh-rerun.yaml) needs its own <service>-token secret when you deploy it.

The runner log shows 401

The log contains 401 (Unauthorized), and the runner never claims a job.

Cause. CircleCI rejected the token. The token was deleted, or the secret holds a token of another class or a mistyped one. A 401 is not a clock problem: a clock that drifted fails the TLS handshake before any request, which gives the error in the next entry.

Fix.

  • Check that the secret <service>-token holds the token of the resource class with the same name as the service. A swapped token does not fail loudly. The runner serves the class of its token, so jobs of the intended class stay queued. On Linux, the token is in the proxy, so look in the log of runners_token-proxy for upstream status 401, and check that its variable for the class names the right secret.
  • Create a new token and rotate it. Refer to Rotate a runner token.

The runner log shows 403 and the proxy log says refused

The runner log contains 403 (Forbidden) for the claim, and the log of runners_token-proxy says claim from <ip> refused.

Cause. The proxy answers a claim only from an address that Swarm DNS lists now for tasks.<service> of a class that it serves, and only once for each container. The reason is in the log line.

Fix.

  • not a runner of any class: the class is not in the proxy (a new class needs its secret <service>-token and, on Linux, its network under token-proxy; refer to Define a class), the proxy is not on the network of the class, or the claim comes from a container that is not a runner.
  • this runner has already claimed a task: the proxy restarted while the runner was idle, the proxy moved to another node and started with a lost state, or a claim of this runner had an unknown outcome and the proxy latched the runner to fail closed. The runner retries every 5 seconds until it is replaced, at its idle timeout. On Linux, replace the idle runners now with docker service update --force --update-parallelism 0 runners_<service>. On Windows, do not: it kills the busy jobs. Remove only the refused containers instead. Refer to Replace refused runners on Windows, A claim whose outcome is unknown, Restart the proxy and Where the proxy runs, and when it moves.
  • too many claims (429), or a 503 with Retry-After: the proxy limits each client IP, and serves at most 512 requests at once. A runner stays far below the limits, so look for a client that polls in a loop, or for a proxy that is overloaded. Refer to Monitor the token proxy and Capacity and concurrency.

The runner log shows x509 certificate errors

The log contains x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid, or x509: certificate signed by unknown authority, and the runner never connects.

Cause. The clock of the node drifted, so TLS to CircleCI fails silently as far as the job is concerned. Or an inspecting proxy re-signs the traffic with a CA that the container does not trust.

Fix. Check the clock with timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized --value, which must print yes, and fix NTP on the node. For the CA of an inspecting proxy or of your CircleCI server, add the CA to your image for the runner and the jobs. The token proxy and the distributors read other stores, so they need their own step. Refer to Proxies and certificate authorities, component by component, Private certificate authorities, and Do proxies and custom certificate authorities work?.

Jobs queue but no runner claims them

Cause. The resource_class in the config does not match a class that has running replicas, or the replicas cannot reach CircleCI.

Fix.

  1. Check that <namespace>/<class> in the job config equals the namespace and the service name.
  2. Check the inventory under Runners in the web app. If the replicas are missing, check that the tasks run and that the egress rules allow the hosts in Egress hosts.
  3. Check that jobs are not in a class that has replicas: 0.

Jobs wait while the runners are idle

The runner inventory shows idle runners, and jobs stay queued.

Cause. The inventory shows running tasks only. Queued tasks are invisible there, and they count against concurrency. A class can sit at the maxConcurrentTasks limit of the resource class (20 by default) or at the runner concurrency of your plan, and jobs for a class that has no runner queue forever and hold concurrency.

Fix. Ask the runner API how many tasks wait, and compare it with the replicas:

$ RUNNER_API=https://runner.circleci.com # the runner API of your installation, for CircleCI server
$ curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" \
 "$RUNNER_API/api/v3/runner/tasks?resource-class=<namespace>/<class>"

A count above 0 with idle replicas points at a limit or at a class name that no service serves. Cancel the tasks of a class that no longer has runners, and ask CircleCI support to raise maxConcurrentTasks. Refer to Capacity and concurrency.

A service shows no logs

docker service logs runners_<service> prints nothing, or prints less than you expect.

Cause. Swarm prunes the old tasks of a slot, and their logs go with them, because every finished job ends a task and the history limit is 2. The command also works only for the local, json-file, and journald drivers, so a service that you moved to a shipping driver has no logs to read back.

Fix. Read docker service ps --no-trunc runners_<service> for the reason a task ended, and docker logs <container> on the node for a task that still has its container. To keep logs, ship them. Refer to Ship the logs.

Error: The swarm does not have a leader

A Swarm command fails with The swarm does not have a leader. It's possible that too few managers are online.

Cause. The managers lost their quorum. A majority of them must be online: two of three, or three of five. Without it, running jobs finish, but no replacement task starts, so the capacity of the cluster drops to zero.

Fix. Bring the managers back, starting with the ones that were stopped last, and check docker node ls on a reachable manager. A manager that is locked needs docker swarm unlock. If the managers are lost for good, recover the cluster from one surviving manager with docker swarm init --force-new-cluster --advertise-addr <manager IP address>. Refer to Back up the managers, and recover and Managers and quorum.

Error: Swarm is encrypted and needs to be unlocked

A Swarm command fails with Swarm is encrypted and needs to be unlocked before it can be used.

Cause. The managers use autolock, and this manager restarted. It stays out of the cluster until someone unlocks it.

Fix. Run docker swarm unlock on the manager and enter the unlock key. Get the key from a manager that is unlocked with docker swarm unlock-key. Refer to Unlock a locked swarm.

A service update is paused or rolled back

docker service update or docker stack deploy stops partway, and docker service inspect --format '{{.UpdateStatus.State}}' runners_<service> prints paused, rollback_started, or rollback_completed. The Message field says which task failed.

Cause. A new task failed to start, for example with exit code 80 after a wrong setting or a missing secret. The stack files set no failure_action, so Swarm pauses the update at the first failure, and the replicas that it did not reach keep the old version.

Fix. Read why the task failed with docker service ps --no-trunc runners_<service>, correct the cause in your stack file, and deploy again with the same list of files. To go back at once, run docker service update --rollback runners_<service>. Refer to Update the images.

A job exits with code 137, or fails to start processes

A task or a step ends with exit code 137, or a build fails with fork: Resource temporarily unavailable or Cannot allocate memory.

Cause. Code 137 is SIGKILL. On Linux the kernel kills a job that exceeds the memory limit of the service, and docker inspect <container> shows OOMKilled: true. The same code appears when a stop outlasts stop_grace_period. A build that starts more processes than limits.pids (4096) fails to fork.

Fix. Raise limits.memory or limits.pids of that class in your stack file, and deploy again. Size the class for its largest job, and keep the reservation equal to the limit. Refer to Size the limits. A job that runs near its limit also needs room on the node.

A job fails with an issue with your infrastructure

The job ends with a message that points at an issue with your infrastructure, and its log stops without an error of its own.

Cause. The runner stopped while it ran the job, or its connection to CircleCI broke. Typical causes are a node that died or rebooted, a stop from outside (an update, a scale-down, or a node drain) that outlasted the grace period or, on Windows, killed the job after about 5 seconds, or an out-of-memory kill.

Fix. Find the container that ran the job with docker service ps --no-trunc runners_<service>: a task that ended with non-zero exit or on a node that is Down names the cause. Self-hosted runners do not retry a job, so rerun it. Refer to Node death and Stop a busy Windows container.

Many jobs fail within seconds on one node

Jobs of a class fail within seconds, or end with no work done, and docker stack ps runners lists many tasks of one node that ended seconds after they started. The node is Ready, and the other nodes are fine.

Cause. A node that is Ready can still fail every job it claims: a full disk, a runner volume whose link current is wrong, a Docker engine in a bad state, a clock that is far off, or a broken route to the registry or to CircleCI after the claim. A failed task is replaced at once, and the replacement claims again, so the broken node takes a large share of the jobs of the class and fails them one after another. Swarm does not see it, because the node answers its heartbeats.

Fix.

  1. Count the tasks that ended in the last minute for each node. A node far above the others is the one:

    $ docker stack ps runners --format '{{.Node}} {{.CurrentState}}' | grep -E ' (Complete|Failed) [0-9]+ seconds? ago' | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
$ docker stack ps runners --no-trunc --format '{{.Node}} {{.Name}} {{.CurrentState}} {{.Error}}' | grep '<node name>' | head -20

  2. Stop it from taking jobs. On Linux, drain it. On Windows, pause it: jobs that fail in seconds free the node quickly, and a drain would kill a good job after about 5 seconds (A Windows node).

    $ docker node update --availability drain <node name>

  3. Find the cause on the node:

    $ df -h /var/lib/docker
$ docker run --rm alpine true
$ docker run --rm -v runners_runner-bin:/v:ro alpine ls -l /v/current
$ docker ps -a --filter 'name=runners_' --format '{{.Names}} {{.Status}}' | head
$ timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized --value

    Read the log of the newest failed container (docker logs <container>) and, on Linux, journalctl -u docker -n 100. A full disk is in Free disk space. A missing current means that the distributor has not installed a runner on this node: read its log (The runner waits for the distributor, and then exits with code 80).

  4. Fix the cause and set the node active. If the cause is not clear, take the node out for good: run docker swarm leave on it, then docker node rm <node name> on a manager, and rebuild it.

  5. Rerun the jobs that failed. Self-hosted runners do not retry a job by themselves.

To see it early, alert on the count in step 1 and keep a canary job for each class.

A task is rejected because the image cannot be pulled

docker service ps shows rejected with No such image or an authentication error.

Cause. The node cannot pull the image: the registry is not reachable, the image is private, or the registry rate limit applies.

Fix. Check egress to the registry, deploy with docker stack deploy --with-registry-auth for a private registry, and use a mirror or authenticated pulls. Refer to Registry needs, and, for a site without a route to the registries, What needs the internet.

Error: This node is not a swarm manager

Swarm commands such as docker stack deploy fail on a worker.

Fix. Run them on a manager. Use docker node ls on a manager to list the managers.

A node cannot join the swarm

docker swarm join times out or fails with a connection error.

Cause. The manager is not reachable on the advertised address and port 2377, or the manager listens on the loopback address only.

Fix. Open the ports in Inter-node ports, and check that the swarm was initialized with a routable --advertise-addr.

Linux

The runner waits for the distributor, and then exits with code 80

The log of a runner container shows circleci-runner-entrypoint: waiting for the runner-distributor of this node to install the runner. After the wait, which is 120 seconds by default, the container exits with code 80 and the message /opt/machine-runner-swarm/current is 'missing': the runner-distributor of this node has not installed the runner. Swarm starts a new container after 10 seconds, and the loop repeats.

Cause. The volume runner-bin of the node has no runner yet. The runner-distributor task of the node is not running, or it cannot download the runner, or it refuses the download. A first deploy and a node that just joined are normal: the wait covers a download of a few seconds, and the next container starts as soon as current exists.

Fix. Check that the distributor runs on that node, and read its log. Each line starts with the task and the node.

$ docker service ps --no-trunc runners_runner-distributor
$ docker service logs --tail 50 runners_runner-distributor

A node that has no task is Down, drained, or not a Linux node. Otherwise the log names the problem: refer to The distributor log shows cannot download and The distributor log shows SHA-256 mismatch. To wait longer, set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_WAIT in the environment of the runner services.

Error: does not match its SHA-256 record

The container exits with code 80 and a message such as /opt/machine-runner-swarm/versions/3.1.13/bin/circleci-runner does not match its SHA-256 record ...: refusing to start.

Cause. The binary in the volume is not the one that the distributor recorded. The install is incomplete, the volume was changed, or the disk is damaged. The entrypoint checks the binary at every start and never runs one that differs. Refer to Runner binary integrity on Linux.

Fix. The distributor compares the active binary with its record at every check, and installs the version again when it differs. To do it now, force an update of the distributor. It downloads the version again on every node, and the next containers start:

$ docker service update --force runners_runner-distributor

If the binary changes again, find out what writes to the volume: a privileged container on the node, or a person with access to it.

The distributor log shows cannot download

A line of docker service logs runners_runner-distributor reads runner-distributor: cannot download <address>, for the file manifest.json or for a tarball such as <version>/circleci-runner_linux_amd64.tar.gz. The distributor keeps the runner that it has and tries again in 5 minutes. Without a runner, the runner containers of the node end in the entry above.

Cause. The node cannot reach circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com or your mirror: an egress rule, a proxy, DNS, or the clock. Or the file is not on the mirror, for example the version that you pinned. An https mirror needs a certificate from a public certificate authority, because the distributor uses the CA bundle of the stock Alpine image. A proxy rarely helps: the wget of the distributor reads only the lowercase http_proxy, sends an https:// URL to the proxy as a plain GET and not as a CONNECT, and ignores no_proxy.

Fix. Download the same file from the node with the same tool:

$ docker run --rm alpine wget -q -O /dev/null https://circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com/circleci-runner/manifest.json && echo reachable

Open the host in Egress hosts, or fix the mirror. A mirror that the node reaches without a proxy is the dependable setup. Refer to Run the downloads from a mirror and Proxies and certificate authorities, component by component.

The distributor log shows SHA-256 mismatch

A line reads runner-distributor: SHA-256 mismatch for circleci-runner_linux_amd64.tar.gz <version>: got <hash>, wanted <hash>: refusing to install. The distributor installs nothing and tries again later.

Cause. The tarball does not have the SHA-256 that the manifest, or your list in MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256, names. The usual causes are a list that lacks the value of one architecture (a fleet with amd64 and arm64 nodes needs both), a mirror whose tarball and manifest do not belong together, and a proxy that changes the download.

Fix. Compare wanted with the SHA-256 of the file that you expect, from the checksums.txt of the release or from the manifest. Correct the list, the mirror, or the proxy. Never copy the got value into the list without checking where the file came from.

The token-proxy service does not start: the image cannot be pulled

docker service ps runners_token-proxy --no-trunc (Windows: runners_token-proxy-windows) shows No such image, manifest unknown, pull access denied, or no matching manifest for <platform>, and the runners get connection errors for token-proxy. The distributor and the runner are unaffected.

Cause. The image is ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy (or what MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE names). The usual causes are a node that cannot reach Docker Hub (a proxy or an allow list), a tag that does not exist (a typo, or edge before the first publication of the main branch), a local image name such as machine-runner-swarm-proxy:dev that exists on another node and not on the node that runs the proxy, and a platform that the tag lacks (Windows on Arm).

Fix. Check the name with docker service inspect runners_token-proxy --format '{{.Spec.TaskTemplate.ContainerSpec.Image}}' and pull it on the node: docker pull <image>. Behind an allow list, add Docker Hub (Egress hosts), or mirror the image and set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE (Upgrade the token proxy). A local build must be on the node that the proxy runs on: build it there, or docker save <image> | ssh <node> docker load. Swarm tries again by itself.

The distributor log shows not adopting it

The log has runner-distributor: current is <version> (major <n>), not 3: not adopting it (MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_MAJOR), or current has SHA-256 <hash>, which no versioned release of the manifest has: not adopting it.

Cause. The first line says that current of CircleCI moved to another major version. The distributor keeps the version that it has, so nothing breaks, and the nodes stay where they are. The second line says that the manifest names no version for current, which happens with a mirror that has an old or edited manifest.json.

Fix. For a new major version, read the changelog of the runner, try it, and then set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_MAJOR or pin the version. Refer to Pin a version. For the second line, copy manifest.json to the mirror again, with the tarball of the version that current names.

Error: must be owned by root and not group/world writable

The container exits with code 80 and a message such as /opt/machine-runner-swarm/versions/3.1.13/bin/circleci-runner must be owned by root and not group/world writable.

Cause. The entrypoint refuses to run a runner that the job user or the runner user can replace. The distributor makes the files of the volume owned by root with the mode 0755, so something changed them.

Fix. On the node, set the owner and the mode again:

$ docker run --rm -v runners_runner-bin:/v alpine sh -c 'chown -R 0:0 /v && chmod -R go-w /v'

Error: jobs cannot be stepped down in this image

The container exits with code 80 and the message jobs cannot be stepped down in this image: it needs sudo or util-linux setpriv.

Cause. The image has neither sudo nor util-linux setpriv, or it has no setpriv and no su to start the runner.

A hardened class (MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO=false) exits with code 80 and the message needs util-linux setpriv with --no-new-privs when the image has no util-linux setpriv, even if it has sudo. The hardened class never steps jobs down with sudo, because a setuid binary could then lift a job to root.

Fix. Add the packages in a derived image. Refer to What an image needs.

Error: failed to remove working directory, permission denied

Every task fails. The runner log shows failed to remove working directory before starting task or failed to remove working directory while cleaning up task, each with permission denied. A could not clean up task line with the same error has the same cause.

Cause. This happens only if someone sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR to true on a Linux service: the entrypoint and the stack files default it to false. The runner removes its working directory itself, as the runner user (uid 2000), but the job user owns that directory and its files. The removal fails even for the first task, because the parent directory belongs to the job user too. The stack files and the entrypoint set the variable to false for this reason.

Fix. Set CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR: "false", or remove the variable so that the entrypoint default applies, and deploy again. A single-task container is discarded after the job, so nothing is lost. In a persistent class, start every job with a step that removes what an earlier job left. Refer to Working directory cleanup.

Permission denied on /opt/machine-runner-swarm with SELinux

On RHEL, a replica reports Permission denied for files under /opt/machine-runner-swarm while SELinux is enforcing.

Cause. Untested: this repository’s CI does not run on RHEL. The runner is in a named volume, and Docker labels the files of a volume for containers in the usual case. A setup where it does not leaves the files with a type that containers may not read. A Swarm service mount has no :z option to relabel them.

Fix. Confirm the denial with sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent, then label the volume on the node. The files that the distributor writes later inherit the label.

$ sudo chcon -R -t container_file_t /var/lib/docker/volumes/runners_runner-bin/_data

Keep SELinux enforcing. Do not disable it to work around the error, and open an issue with the avc line if you needed this.

Warning: sudo unable to send audit message

Every sudo call in a job prints unable to send audit message.

Cause. The AUDIT_WRITE capability is dropped.

Fix. Keep AUDIT_WRITE out of cap_drop. A hardened class keeps it in cap_add.

Jobs in the hardened class cannot install packages

apt-get install fails with Permission denied, or sudo reports that the user may not run sudo.

Cause. The hardened class steps jobs down with setpriv --no-new-privs, so sudo cannot raise the job user, by design.

Fix. Build the tools into the image. Refer to Bring your own image.

Cannot connect to the Docker daemon in a job

docker build fails with Cannot connect to the Docker daemon.

Cause. The class does not mount a Docker engine, by design.

Fix. Use the opt-in class, or a daemonless builder. Refer to Docker Builds.

Permission denied on the Docker socket in a docker-build job

A job on a docker-build class fails with permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket at unix:///var/run/docker.sock.

Cause. The entrypoint adds the job user to the group of the mounted socket so that the job can use it, but it skips a socket whose group id is 0, because group 0 is root’s group and giving the job user that group would be wrong. A host whose socket is owned by root:root therefore leaves the job user without access.

Fix. Give the socket on the host a group that is not root, normally docker. With systemd, the socket unit of Docker sets it with SocketGroup=docker. Check with stat -c '%U:%G %g' /var/run/docker.sock, which must show a group id above 0, and deploy again so that the new containers pick it up. Refer to Docker Builds.

The disk fills up

A task fails with no space left on device, Docker commands on the node fail, or the node stops taking jobs.

Cause. Each finished job leaves a stopped container, and Swarm keeps the last five tasks of every slot by default. Images, build cache, and logs add to it.

Fix. Stop the node from taking jobs, free the space, and set the history limit. The steps, and the schedule that keeps it from happening again, are in Free disk space. A node that fails jobs because its disk is full can also look like Many jobs fail within seconds on one node.

Windows

Error: 0xc0370101

A task is rejected with The container operating system does not match the host operating system.

Cause. The image build is newer than the host build. A Server 2022 host runs only ltsc2022 images, and a Server 2025 host runs ltsc2025 and ltsc2022 images. The placement labels normally keep a service off a node that cannot run its image, so look for a node that carries a label it should not.

Fix. Use an image tag that the host can run, and label the node with the matching machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022 and windows-ltsc2025 capabilities. Refer to Image tags and host builds.

The runner never claims a job

The container runs and logs the start-up lines, but the runner never claims a job and logs no clear error.

Cause. The runner creates a symbolic link when it installs the task agent. Without the SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege, it retries the download forever. This happens when the container runs as a user other than ContainerAdministrator.

Fix. Never set user: in a Windows service, and never change USER in a derived image.

The Windows runner fails to start: cannot access path current

docker service ps --no-trunc runners_windows-default shows tasks that fail with cannot access path ...\runner-bin\_data\current (or ...\git\current) or with invalid mount config, and Swarm starts the next task after 10 seconds.

Cause. The service runner-distributor-windows has not flipped the links current and git\current of the volume on this node yet. This is normal on a new node, because the first download of the runner and of portable Git takes a few minutes. It lasts when the distributor cannot install.

Fix. Read the log of the distributor: docker service logs runners_runner-distributor-windows. A SHA-256 mismatch, a cannot download line, or not adopting it names the cause. The service must run on the node: docker service ps runners_runner-distributor-windows needs a task there, so the node must carry the label machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true, and the base image must be pulled. On a host behind a proxy, set HTTPS_PROXY on the distributor service (it reads HTTPS_PROXY only, and no NO_PROXY). For a site without internet access, refer to Upgrade the runner on Windows.

The distributor of Windows keeps a version that should be gone

The log says circleci-runner <version> is in use: removing it at a later check.

Cause. Windows cannot remove files that a running container uses. A job on that version is still running.

Fix. None needed: the distributor removes the version at a later check, when the job has ended.

Error: could not find the system’s IP address

docker swarm init fails with could not find the system's IP address - specify one with --advertise-addr.

Fix. Always pass the IPv4 address of the host: docker swarm init --advertise-addr <host IPv4 address>. A host with several network adapters needs it too, and Setup.ps1 -InitSwarm requires -AdvertiseAddr.

Downloads fail right after docker swarm init

Outbound connections fail with Unable to connect to the remote server or no such host for a few seconds after you create the swarm.

Fix. Pull the images first, and run docker swarm init last. The distributor retries its downloads.

Windows container exits with code 3221225786 after a stop

A job ends about 5 seconds after a rolling update, a scale down, a node drain, or docker stop. docker service ps --no-trunc shows task: non-zero exit (3221225786), which is 0xC000013A.

Cause. The container was stopped from outside while it ran a job, and Windows gives a stock Server Core container about 5 seconds, whatever stop_grace_period says. A job that finishes by itself does not end this way.

Fix. Rerun the interrupted jobs, and change a service only while its class runs no job. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container.

Error: hcs::System::Start: context deadline exceeded

A Windows container does not start, and docker service ps --no-trunc shows hcs::System::Start: context deadline exceeded.

Cause. One cause is an image build that replaced a registry key. New-Item -Force on an existing key deletes its values and subkeys. On HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\cexecsvc, it removes the definition of the container exec service, and the container cannot start.

Fix. Rebuild the image, and set registry values with reg add or Set-ItemProperty, which only set a value. Never use New-Item -Force on an existing registry key.

Workspaces fail because tar or gzip is missing

persist_to_workspace or attach_workspace reports a missing tar or gzip.

Cause. The Git mount is missing, or the PATH of the service does not include C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin. The PATH of a service replaces the one of the image.

Fix. Keep both mounts and the full PATH from the shipped file.

tar fails with Cannot stat when you test it by hand

You run C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin\tar.exe in a container with a backslash path, and it fails with Cannot stat.

Cause. The task agent starts this tar.exe from the root of the drive, with --force-local, and with forward-slash operands that are relative to the root. For C:\cci\w\ws, it passes cci/w/ws. It never passes a backslash operand, which this tar does not accept.

Fix. Use the same form in your test. A workspace step that fails in a job is more likely a missing tar or gzip on the PATH, as in the previous entry.

Overlay network creation fails

Cause. On a host with one network adapter, an existing transparent network can block the creation of overlay networks.

Fix. Refer to the Microsoft documentation on Windows container networking, and move the transparent network to a second adapter or remove it.

The first task on a host takes a long time

Cause. The node pulls the Server Core image, which is about 2.2 GB compressed, when the first task lands there.

Fix. Run docker pull for the image on each node before you deploy.

Setup.ps1 reports CHECK windows-server FAIL

Cause. The helper supports Windows Server 2022 (build 20348) and 2025 (build 26100), and the host is another version or a client edition.

Fix. Use a Server 2022 or 2025 host. Server 2019 is untested: the stack files have no label or placement for it, so a 2019 node needs your own image tag, label, and constraint.

Collect information for a bug report

Gather the output of these commands. Remove tokens before you share it.

$ docker version
$ docker node ls
$ docker stack ps runners --no-trunc
$ docker service logs --tail 200 runners_<service>
$ docker service logs --tail 200 runners_token-proxy

On Linux, include the runner version and the log of the distributor: docker run --rm -v runners_runner-bin:/v:ro alpine cat /v/current/VERSION on the node, and docker service logs --tail 100 runners_runner-distributor. On Windows, include the log of runner-distributor-windows: docker service logs --tail 100 runners_runner-distributor-windows. Then open an issue.
